lines.text: Your smoke detector doesn't smell smoke. It does something much stranger.
Inside are two different tricks. One uses a speck of radioactive metal. The other uses light.
Trick one: ionization. A speck of americium charges the air, so a tiny current flows between two plates.
Smoke particles grab those ions and block the current. When it drops, the alarm sounds.
Trick two, light. An LED shines past a sensor that can't see it. No smoke, no signal.
When smoke drifts in, it scatters the beam onto the sensor. Now it sees light, and the alarm sounds.
Which is better? Ionization reacts fastest to flaming fires. Photoelectric wins on slow, smoldering ones.
That's why the safest choice is both, or a dual sensor alarm.
And the three a.m. chirp? Batteries weaken in the cold, and your house is coolest before dawn.
Press test every month, and read the date on the back: detectors expire after ten years.
Watch again, and spot the blocked ions.
